title: Caring for yourself as a carer
word: Caring for yourself as a carer

segments.voice: Yesterday: compassion in medicine, and the line care heals. Did a health worker get a bit of kindness back from you? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

The phone lights up at the edge of the bed: Mom needs her pills sorted, the kids need lunches, a friend needs a call back, and work needs that thing by noon. Somewhere at the very bottom of the list, below the dog's vet appointment, there's a line that never quite gets written: rest. People who look after others, a parent, a nurse, someone caring for a sick partner, may know the shape of that list. Yesterday was about the care that heals. Today asks a quieter question: who's on the list of people that care is for?
screen: `PILLS, LUNCHES, CALLS, NOON.` → `REST: NEVER WRITTEN DOWN.` → `WHO IS THE CARE FOR?`

segments.voice: First, a circle with you in it. A few days ago, the Stoic Hierocles drew his circles of concern: family, neighbors, humanity. Look again at the picture. At the very center, he put the self. Not to crown it, but because it's where every ring starts. A caregiver who leaves the center empty has nothing for the rings to grow from. Second, a teacher who sent his friends to rest. In the Gospel of Mark, the disciples come back from their work, crowded and busy, and Jesus says, in the King James words: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." Mark adds the reason: so many were coming and going that they had no time even to eat. Rest, given as an instruction, in the middle of the work. Third, kindness that starts at home. In the Visuddhimagga, the Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa describes developing loving-kindness by beginning with oneself, then moving out to others. The reasoning he gives: once you see that you want to be happy, you can see that others want it too. Fourth, the modern version. Kristin Neff's research on self-compassion describes treating yourself with the kindness you would give a friend, recognizing that struggle is part of being human, and noticing pain without being swept away. Self-compassion, in that account, isn't selfishness, and it isn't giving up on others. It's including one more person in the care: the one doing the caring. So when the wish goes out, may they be well, there's room for two more words. Me too.
screen: `THE SELF AT THE CENTER.` · `COME APART AND REST A WHILE.` · `KINDNESS BEGINS WITH ONESELF.` · then, large: `ONE MORE PERSON IN THE CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short rest with permission. Let the body get as comfortable as it can. Drop the shoulders. Unclench the jaw. Let the breath go slow. Bring to mind the people you look after, one by one, briefly, and let them rest in the back of your mind. Then turn the same care toward yourself: the hands that do the carrying, the tired back, the full head. If it helps, put a hand on your chest. For this short time, nobody needs anything from you. The bell holds the time.
Caring for yourself as a carer. Compassion includes the one who gives it. Today's word.
screen: `CARING FOR YOURSELF AS A CARER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: me too. Today, put rest on the list: find ten minutes to stop, with nothing to fix and nobody to help, and treat them as part of the care. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In loving-kindness practice as Buddhaghosa describes it, the wish for well-being begins with oneself before moving outward, and self-compassion programs teach caregivers to offer themselves the kindness they give others.
